tagline: An Andaman coast town of hot springs, Koh Phayam, and the Myanmar border, known for eight months of rain and four of sun
introHtml:
Ranong is a long, narrow province on the upper Andaman coast, famous as the rainiest place in Thailand. The small town sits in a valley around the natural Raksawarin hot springs in the center, with rows of old Hokkien Chinese shophouses that recall the tin-mining era.

Head out toward the sea and there are piers to Koh Phayam and Koh Chang, both still quiet, with clear water and empty beaches that reward a long, slow stay. Across from Pak Nam Ranong sits Kawthaung in Myanmar, where people cross over to walk the markets and renew visas. People come to Ranong to soak in the hot springs, eat seafood, and reach the islands without fighting anyone for space.
bestTime: November–March brings less rain and calm seas, ideal for Koh Phayam and Koh Chang. Soaking in the hot springs and sightseeing in town work year-round.

highlights.name: Raksawarin Hot Springs
highlights.blurb: A natural hot spring in the center of Ranong town, with water bubbling up from underground all day. There are foot-soaking pools and mineral bathhouses, and it's the first thing most people picture when they think of Ranong.

highlights.name: Koh Phayam
highlights.blurb: A still-quiet island in the Andaman Sea with Ao Yai and Ao Khao Kwai beaches and clear water. No cars run here, so you get around mainly by motorbike, and it's made for an easy stay of several days.

highlights.name: Old Shophouses and Ranong Town
highlights.blurb: The town has old Hokkien Chinese shophouses and mansions from the tin-mining era, such as Baan Thian Sue and the Ranong Governor's Residence. You can walk around and take in the old architecture in town.

highlights.name: Pak Nam Ranong and the Kawthaung Border
highlights.blurb: Pak Nam Ranong sits across from the town of Kawthaung in Myanmar. There's a fish-market pier for watching the fishing boats and seafood stalls, and you can take a boat across to walk the markets on the Myanmar side.

highlights.name: Phukao Ya and Khao Fachi Viewpoint
highlights.blurb: Phukao Ya is an open grassy hill that changes color with the seasons, while Khao Fachi is a viewpoint over the mouth of the Kraburi River and the Myanmar side. Both are best in the early morning.

highlights.name: Ranong Cashew Nuts
highlights.blurb: Ranong grows a lot of cashews, and roasted and processed cashew nuts are a well-known local souvenir. You can buy them in town and at roadside shops.

foodScene.name: Pak Nam Seafood
foodScene.note: Right on the Andaman, there are fresh prawns, crab, fish, and shellfish from Pak Nam Ranong. Seafood spots in town and along the water cook it every way — steamed, stir-fried, and in tom yum.

foodScene.name: Ranong Oysters
foodScene.note: The mouth of the Kraburi River raises large, meaty oysters. Eat them raw with the usual sides or battered and fried — a local specialty you'll find all over town.

foodScene.name: Dim Sum and Old-Style Coffee
foodScene.note: With its Hokkien Chinese roots, Ranong has morning dim sum and old-style coffee shops. Sit down for steamed buns, dumplings, and kopi before you head out.

foodScene.name: Cashew Nuts
foodScene.note: The province's signature souvenir comes salted, honey-roasted, and pan-roasted. Pick some up from shops in town and roadside stalls near the hot springs.

foodScene.name: Khanom Jeen and Southern Food
foodScene.note: Bold southern dishes are everywhere in town — khanom jeen with curry, gaeng tai pla, gaeng leuang, and fresh raw vegetables. This is the everyday food of Ranong locals.

foodScene.name: Fish-Market Seafood
foodScene.note: At Pak Nam Ranong there's a fish-market pier selling seafood fresh off the boats. Buy prawns, crab, and fish to have a restaurant cook, or take them home, at a fair price.

foodScene.name: Burmese Food and Border Goods
foodScene.note: Close to the Kawthaung border, the town's markets mix in food and dried goods from the Myanmar side — fried snacks, pickled items, and spices worth a taste.

attractions.name: Raksawarin Hot Springs
attractions.blurb: A natural hot spring in the center of town where the water bubbles up nonstop, with foot-soaking pools and mineral bathhouses set in a shady public park.

attractions.name: Koh Phayam
attractions.blurb: A still-quiet Andaman island with Ao Yai and Ao Khao Kwai bays, clear water, and no cars — made for several days of lazing on the beach.

attractions.name: Koh Chang Ranong
attractions.blurb: A small island near Koh Phayam with a laid-back feel, quiet beaches, and simple, rustic stays — for people who really want some peace.

attractions.name: Ngao Waterfall
attractions.blurb: A tall waterfall in the national park, visible from the roadside, where you can walk in for a swim. It's shady and not far from town.

attractions.name: Ranong Governor's Residence and Old Houses
attractions.blurb: Old Chinese-style buildings and mansions from the era of the Khaw Soo Cheang governing family, telling the story of Ranong's tin-mining days.

attractions.name: Rattanarangsan Palace (Replica)
attractions.blurb: A brown wooden house in the center of town built as a replica of the original palace, where you can take in the timber architecture and the story of Ranong.

attractions.name: Phukao Ya and Khao Fachi
attractions.blurb: An open grassy hill and a viewpoint over the mouth of the Kraburi River and the Myanmar side — good for the view and photos in the early morning.

attractions.name: Pak Nam Ranong and the Fish-Market Pier
attractions.blurb: A fishing pier across from Kawthaung in Myanmar, where you can watch the boats come and go, walk the seafood market, and catch a boat across to the Myanmar side.

itineraryIdeas: Ranong 2D1N — hot springs, old town, Pak Nam
Ranong island run — Koh Phayam and Koh Chang for a long stay
Ranong nature route — Ngao Waterfall, Phukao Ya, Khao Fachi
Ranong day trip — soak in the hot springs and eat seafood
Ranong to Chumphon — cross the peninsula from the Andaman to the Gulf
Ranong to Phang-nga — work down the Andaman coast
